subject: Biology
title: Dominant and Recessive Traits
description: A micro-lesson that makes Dominant and Recessive Traits usable.

hook.text: You have two copies of every gene—one from each parent. Sometimes one copy overrules the other.

buildup.text: A dominant allele shows its trait even with one copy. A recessive allele needs two copies.

discovery.text: Two brown-eyed parents can have a blue-eyed child if both carry a hidden recessive allele.

twist.text: Dominant doesn't mean better or more common. It just means it masks the recessive form.

climax.text: Mendel's ratios—3 to 1 in the second generation—revealed this hidden pattern.

punchline.text: One copy hides. Two copies reveal.

quiz.question: When does a recessive trait appear?
options: When two recessive alleles are present
When one recessive allele is present
When no dominant allele exists in the population

details.summary: Dominant alleles produce their phenotype when just one copy is present, while recessive alleles require two copies. This explains why carriers of recessive conditions like cystic fibrosis show no symptoms yet can pass the allele to children.
details.whyItMatters: Dominance and recessiveness are the foundation of genetic inheritance. They explain why traits skip generations, why genetic diseases persist in populations, and how parents without symptoms can have affected children.
takeaways: A single dominant allele is sufficient to express the trait
Recessive traits appear only when both alleles are recessive
Carriers have one recessive allele but show no symptoms

faq.question: How can two healthy parents have a child with a genetic disease?
faq.answer: Both parents can be carriers, each with one normal dominant allele and one disease recessive allele. They show no symptoms, but each child has a 25 percent chance of inheriting both recessive copies and expressing the disease.

faq.question: Is dominant always better than recessive?
faq.answer: No. Dominant and recessive describe how alleles interact, not whether they are beneficial. Huntington's disease is caused by a dominant allele that is clearly harmful. Sickle cell carriers with one recessive allele actually gain malaria resistance.
